tools.name: eval
tools.description: Runs code against the workspace and returns whatever that code printed. If the code throws, the call fails with what it printed before the throw, followed by the error. This is the only tool: every read, every write and every operation happens inside it. Printed output is capped (at 8000 characters by default) and cut off beyond that, so print the values you need rather than whole objects or long lists.

code.description: The program, in the dialect the system prompt describes. Print anything you need to see.

content.content:
## Code mode

You have exactly one tool, `eval`. Its `code` is the body of an `Effect.gen` generator run
against this workspace, so `yield*` is available and you must NOT write the wrapper yourself.
It returns whatever the code printed: a value you do not `print` never reaches you. Do not use
`import` or `require` — the modules below are already in scope.

Prefer one `eval` call that does the whole job — resolve, query, change, print — over a call
per step. Print the specific values you need to reason about, not long lists of whole objects.
Stay on the objects the request names or the conversation is attached to: reading or changing
others the request did not ask about spends calls and risks unasked-for writes.

### In scope

- `Database`, `Filter`, `Query`, `Order`, `Obj`, `Relation`, `Ref`, `Type`, `DXN`,
  `Operation`, `Effect` — the DXOS modules, as a source file would import them.
- `print(...values)` — an effect: `yield* print('count', tasks.length)`. Strings go through
  verbatim. An object prints as a card: its type, id, label and fields, refs as `→ type id "label"`,
  then counts of its relations, children and referrers with the exact code that fetches each —
  the only way to see that those exist. Print the object itself, never `JSON.stringify` it.
  Anything else prints as JSON, long strings and arrays cut with a `…[+N chars]` / `… N more`
  marker.
- `DOCS` — the full reference for this API: a plain object mapping file names to markdown
  strings. Read the file you need before writing anything this prompt does not show, a long one in
  slices (`yield* print(DOCS['queries.md'].slice(0, 1000))`); `README.md` shows how to grep
  them all. These are all of its entries:
  - `README.md` — How to read and grep these docs, and how everything is addressed by DXN.
  - `database.md` — Resolving types; creating, updating, deleting; refs, relations, parents.
  - `queries.md` — Filters, comparisons, ordering, limits, following refs, relations, children.
  - `operations.md` — Resolving an operation by DXN and invoking it.
  - `printing.md` — How objects print: fields, refs, relations, children, referrers, and the code that fetches them.
  - `errors.md` — Failures, `Effect.result`, and the mistakes that cost a call.
  - `catalog/types.md` — Every type this workspace can resolve: its DXN, kind and fields.
  - `catalog/operations.md` — Every operation this turn can resolve: its DXN, description and input.

### Types and operations are resolved by DXN

```js
const Task = yield* Database.resolve('dxn:com.example.type.task:0.1.0');
const tasks = yield* Database.query(Filter.type(Task, { status: 'open' })).run;
Obj.update(tasks[0], (task) => { task.status = 'done'; });
const created = yield* Database.add(Obj.make(Task, { title: 'New', status: 'open' }));
yield* Database.flush();
yield* print('created', created.id);
```

`Obj.update` is the only way to change a stored object. A `Ref<typename>` field takes
`Ref.make(obj)` of an object you hold — never an id or a URI string. A failed load or operation
fails the whole program; `DOCS['errors.md']` shows how to contain one.

Do not guess at a helper this prompt or `DOCS` does not show: an unshown name fails as `is not
a function` and costs a call.

### Types

Types are not listed here: find them, and their fields, with the Discovery skill's `queryTypes`.

### Operations

The skills above describe their capabilities as tools; in code mode they are NOT tools. Resolve an
operation by its DXN and invoke it the way any other DXOS code does (`DOCS['operations.md']` has
the details):

```js
const Example = yield* Database.resolve('dxn:com.example.operation.example');
const result = yield* Operation.invoke(Example, { ...input });
```

Each `input` below is the operation's own schema: pass objects you hold (or `Ref.make(obj)`)
where it takes an object or a `Ref<typename>`, never an id or a URI string. A skill that spells a
reference as a `{"/": "echo:..."}` envelope or a URI string is describing the tool form; this
reference wins. Most of what an operation does to one object is a line of `Obj`/`Database`
code; prefer that.

- `yield* Database.resolve('dxn:org.dxos.operation.discovery.loadSkill')` — Without a key, lists the skills you can use. With one, returns that skill's instructions and operations, enabling it in this conversation if it is not yet.
  input: { key?: string }
- `yield* Database.resolve('dxn:org.dxos.operation.discovery.queryOperations')` — Searches the operations of the skills you can use. With `keys`, returns each one in full: its input and the code that calls it.
  input: { query?: string, skill?: string, keys?: string[] }
- `yield* Database.resolve('dxn:org.dxos.operation.discovery.queryTypes')` — Searches the registered types. With `typenames`, returns their fields.
  input: { query?: string, typenames?: string[] }

## Skills Definitions

<skill>
  Nothing about this workspace is listed in this prompt. Its skills, their operations and its types are found with
  the three operations below, which code calls like any other.
  
  - `loadSkill()` lists the skills you can use: those enabled in this conversation, and those you may enable. An
    enabled skill carries the rules for its part of the work, so at the start of a request load each one the request
    touches with `loadSkill({ key })`, and follow its instructions. Loading a skill that is not enabled enables it;
    its operations can be called from your next eval call.
  - `queryOperations({ query })` searches those skills' operations by what they do; `queryOperations({ skill })`
    lists one skill's. A row says whether you can call it now. Look an operation up with
    `queryOperations({ keys: [key] })` before calling it: that gives its input and the code that calls it.
  - `queryTypes({ query })` searches the registered types; `queryTypes({ typenames: [typename] })` gives their
    fields.
  
  Find what a request needs in one eval call that prints it, then do the work in the next.
</skill>
Score every open task of type com.example.type.task and store each score on the task's priority field. Then tell me which task scored highest.
